questoes.pergunta: Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent. You are building a patient billing support agent for a regional hospital network with the Claude Agent SDK. It handles high-ambiguity requests such as disputed bills, refunds for cancelled procedures, and patient-portal account issues through custom MCP tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human), with a target of 80%+ first-contact resolution while knowing when to escalate. The main agent hands complex bill investigations to a billing-research subagent through the Task tool. Logs show two problems: the subagent's first reply often says "no account or order specified" although the patient gave both earlier and get_customer already verified them, and when the subagent is invoked a second time in the same case it repeats lookups it already completed. Which TWO changes address these problems? Choose TWO.
opcoes: Have the subagent call get_customer and lookup_order at the start of each invocation, so that it rebuilds the case from the backend.
Include the verified customer ID, the order numbers, and the patient's own description of the dispute in the Task prompt for the subagent.
Add to the subagent's system prompt that the main agent has already verified the patient and order, so that it stops asking for them.
Configure the subagent to share the main agent's session, so that it inherits the patient's messages and the already verified IDs on its own.
On each later invocation, pass the subagent's earlier findings back in its prompt, because it keeps nothing from a previous invocation.
questoes.explicacao: Subagents run with isolated context: they do not inherit the coordinator's conversation history and do not remember earlier invocations. Everything the subagent needs for this case (verified IDs, order numbers, the patient's stated dispute, and its own earlier findings) has to be written explicitly into the Task prompt.
feedbacks: Tempting because the subagent has the tools, but it repeats verified lookups, adds latency, and still cannot recover what the patient said about the dispute, which exists only in the main conversation.
Correct. The Task prompt is the subagent's only view of the case, so the verified IDs and the patient's description must be passed in it.
This is the implicit-context anti-pattern: telling the subagent that the work was done does not give it the data, so it will ask again or fill the gaps with guesses.

Tempting because it would fix both symptoms at once, but subagents do not inherit or share the parent's conversation; no setting makes the history flow in by itself. The context has to be passed in the prompt.
Correct. Each invocation starts fresh, so prior findings must be passed back explicitly to avoid repeating completed lookups.

questoes.pergunta: In the hospital network's patient billing agent, patients upload the text of insurer letters and ask the agent to explain each charge. Some insurers print the adjustment reason next to each line item; others print only a code on each line (for example "CO-97") and explain all codes in a remarks section at the end of the letter. The agent explains 94% of charges correctly in the first layout but only 61% in the second, often saying "no reason given". Letters come from more than 40 insurers, and there is no time to build insurer-specific parsers this quarter. What is the most effective fix?
opcoes: Add an instruction to the system prompt telling the agent to read the entire letter carefully before it explains any of the charges.
Build a preprocessing step that rewrites each letter into one standard layout using a template per insurer before the agent sees it.
Add few-shot examples of both layouts, including one where a line's code is resolved from the remarks section at the end of the letter.
Route letters that use end-of-letter codes to billing staff, and let the agent explain only letters that state each reason inline.
questoes.explicacao: The agent fails on one document structure: the reason is not next to the line but in a separate section that must be linked back by code. Few-shot examples that show both structures, including how to resolve a code from the remarks section, teach the model to handle the variation across insurers without per-insurer engineering.
feedbacks: Tempting as a cheap prompt change, but a general instruction to read carefully does not show the model how to link a line's code to its explanation at the end of the letter.
This would work in principle, but templates for 40+ insurers are exactly the per-insurer engineering the team cannot build this quarter; it is over-engineering for the constraint.
Correct. Examples that demonstrate both structures teach the model where to find the reason when it is not inline.
This pushes a large share of the work to staff and lowers first-contact resolution, when the agent can learn the second layout from examples.

questoes.pergunta: The hospital network runs a nightly Claude-based quality pass over closed support conversations and sends flagged issues to supervisors. The prompt says: "Review the conversation and flag any problems. Only report issues you are highly confident about." Supervisors receive about 45 flags per day; roughly 70% concern wording or greeting style and are dismissed, and serious issues, such as balance details disclosed before identity verification or refunds promised outside policy, get lost among them. What is the most effective first step?
opcoes: Raise the confidence bar in the prompt so that only findings the model rates 9 or 10 out of 10 are sent to the supervisors each night.
Add an independent second Claude pass that re-reads each flag and discards those it judges less important before supervisors see it.
Group the flags by conversation and sort them by severity, so that supervisors review the most serious flags first each morning.
Define what to report, such as disclosures before identity checks or out-of-policy promises, and what to skip, such as wording.
questoes.explicacao: The prompt never says which issues matter, so the model flags whatever looks imperfect. Specific categorical criteria (report disclosures before verification and out-of-policy commitments; skip style) improve precision directly, while confidence-based filtering does not, because the model is equally confident about the style comments.
feedbacks: This is confidence-based filtering, the instruction that is already failing: the style flags are not low-confidence, they are out of scope, so a higher bar does not remove them.
Over-engineering: a second pass inherits the same missing criteria and adds cost before the cheaper fix, defining what to report, has been tried.
Sorting helps supervisors triage but leaves 70% of the flags as noise, so it treats the symptom without improving the review's precision.
Correct. Explicit report/skip criteria tell the model what an issue is, which is what improves precision.

questoes.pergunta: In the hospital network's patient billing agent, the coordinator uses three subagents: billing-research (reads orders and invoices), refund-execution (calls process_refund), and patient-communication (drafts messages to patients). All three are configured with the same 11 MCP tools. In testing, the patient-communication subagent called process_refund twice while drafting a message about a refund that was still pending review. Design 1 keeps all tools on every subagent and lists in each system prompt the tools it must not use. Design 2 gives each subagent only the tools its role needs. Which design should you choose?
opcoes: Design 1, because keeping the full tool set lets each subagent handle unexpected needs without a round trip to the coordinator.
Design 1, with an explicit list of forbidden tools repeated at the end of each prompt, where recent instructions get more attention.
Design 2, because a subagent cannot misuse a tool it does not have, and a smaller tool set also makes its tool choices more reliable.
Design 2 only for the patient-communication subagent, while the other two subagents keep all 11 tools for the sake of flexibility.
questoes.explicacao: The communication subagent misused a tool outside its specialization. Restricting each subagent to the tools relevant to its role removes the possibility of cross-role misuse and, by shrinking the choice set, improves selection reliability; a prompt-level ban is only probabilistic.
feedbacks: Flexibility is the argument for over-provisioning, but it is exactly what let a drafting agent trigger a refund; unexpected needs should go back through the coordinator.
Tempting because instruction placement does matter, but a forbidden-tools list is still prompt-based guidance with a non-zero failure rate for an action with financial consequences.
Correct. Scoped tool access per role prevents cross-specialization misuse and reduces decision complexity.
Partially right, but the research subagent has no reason to hold process_refund either; the same misuse can reappear in any over-provisioned subagent.

questoes.pergunta: The engineers who build the hospital network's billing agent also use Claude Code to debug it against a staging billing MCP server. Today only one engineer has the server, configured in his ~/.claude.json with the staging token written in it. The new requirement: every engineer who clones the agent's repository gets the server automatically, and no credential is ever committed. What should you change?
opcoes: Add the server to the repository's .mcp.json with the staging token included, since the repository is private and limited to engineers.
Document the server entry in the README so that each engineer copies it into their own ~/.claude.json together with a personal token.
Add the server to the repository's .mcp.json and reference the token as ${BILLING_STAGING_TOKEN}, set in each engineer's environment.
Commit a setup script that writes the server entry and a token from the team vault into each engineer's ~/.claude.json on first run.
questoes.explicacao: Shared team tooling belongs in the project-scoped .mcp.json, which is versioned and therefore available to everyone who clones the repository. Environment variable expansion such as ${BILLING_STAGING_TOKEN} keeps the secret out of version control while each engineer supplies it locally.
feedbacks: Project scope is right, but committing the token violates the requirement; a private repository still spreads the secret to every clone, fork, and backup.
User-level ~/.claude.json is for personal or experimental servers; a manual copy step is not "automatic" and drifts as the entry changes.
Correct. Project-scoped .mcp.json shares the server, and ${VAR} expansion keeps the credential out of the repository.
Over-engineered and still user-scoped: the script recreates per-user configuration instead of using the project-level file designed for shared servers.

questoes.pergunta: In the hospital network's patient billing agent, a patient writes: "I was charged twice for my March 3 MRI copay, the refund for my cancelled March 10 sleep study never arrived, and I can't log in to the portal." The logs show get_customer, then lookup_order for the MRI, then process_refund for the duplicate copay, and finally a response with stop_reason "end_turn": "Your duplicate copay has been refunded. Is there anything else?" The same pattern appears in 38% of messages that raise several issues. What is the most likely root cause?
opcoes: lookup_order returns only one order per call, so the agent cannot retrieve the second order within the same response to the patient.
The loop stops at the first "end_turn", and it should keep running until each concern in the patient's message has been resolved.
The conversation history is not resent with the tool results, so the agent loses the rest of the message after its first tool call.
The agent is not guided to split a message into separate issues and investigate each one before composing one combined resolution.
questoes.explicacao: The agent treats a multi-concern message as a single request and stops after resolving the first item. The fix is to decompose the request into distinct issues, investigate each (in parallel where possible, using the shared context), and then synthesize one unified resolution.
feedbacks: Even if each call returns one order, the agent can call lookup_order again in the next iteration; the logs show it never tried.
Stopping on "end_turn" is correct loop control; the model chose to finish because it was never guided to treat the message as three issues.
If history were missing, the agent would lose the whole case after its first call, not handle one issue correctly and skip the rest; the symptom is selective, not total.
Correct. Without decomposition into distinct items, the agent resolves the first issue and closes the turn.

questoes.pergunta: In the hospital network's patient billing agent, process_refund returns {"isError": true, "content": "Refund could not be processed"} for every failure, and a wrapper retries any isError response up to three times with backoff before the agent replies. Logs show that 22% of refund failures are rejections because the 120-day refund window has passed; each is retried three times, adds about 40 seconds, and ends with the patient being told about "a temporary system issue". What is the flaw in this implementation?
opcoes: The backoff interval is too short for the payment gateway, so the retries hit the same outage; the interval should be several minutes.
The retries happen in the wrapper, and retry decisions should instead be left to the model, which can read the error text on its next turn.
The error has no category or retryable flag, so a policy rejection that can never succeed looks the same as a transient outage.
Policy rejections should return isError false with an empty result, so that the agent does not treat them as failures of the refund tool.
questoes.explicacao: A uniform error hides whether a failure is transient or a business-rule violation. Returning structured metadata such as errorCategory "business", isRetryable false, and a patient-friendly explanation lets the wrapper skip pointless retries and lets the agent explain the 120-day rule instead of blaming the system.
feedbacks: This assumes the failures are outages; for policy rejections no interval helps, because the outcome will never change on retry.
Moving the decision to the model does not help when the error text is the same generic message for every failure; the missing piece is the metadata, not who decides.
Correct. Without errorCategory and isRetryable, non-retryable business errors are retried and misreported.
This is silent suppression: returning a policy rejection as success hides the reason from the agent, which then cannot explain the rule to the patient.

questoes.pergunta: In the hospital network's patient billing agent, a hook intercepts every outgoing process_refund call and denies it when the amount exceeds $750, returning a message telling the agent to use escalate_to_human. The system prompt also states the $750 limit. In one month there were 2,340 refund calls; 61 were above $750, the hook denied all 61, and in 58 of them the agent then escalated. A teammate argues that the 61 attempts prove the hook is not working. Which statement about this behavior is correct?
opcoes: The 61 attempts show the model ignores the limit, so the hook should be replaced by few-shot examples that teach the $750 rule.
The hook makes the prompt rule redundant, so the limit can be removed from the system prompt without changing the outcome.
The hook did its job: no refund above $750 was executed, even though the model still attempted some, which a prompt cannot rule out.
The 3 cases without escalation show the hook failed there, so a PostToolUse hook should also reverse refunds above $750 afterward.
questoes.explicacao: A hook that intercepts outgoing tool calls gives a deterministic guarantee: every call above the threshold was blocked. The model's occasional attempts are the expected residue of probabilistic prompt compliance, which is why the hook exists; the three non-escalations are a separate follow-up, not a hook failure.
feedbacks: Replacing a deterministic block with examples moves the rule back to probabilistic compliance, the opposite of what a financial limit requires.
Tempting because the hook does guarantee the outcome, but the prompt still guides the agent to escalate directly; removing it would increase blocked attempts and detours.
Correct. Interception hooks enforce the rule regardless of what the model attempts.
The hook denied all 61 calls, so nothing above $750 executed and there is nothing to reverse; the three cases concern what the agent did next, not enforcement.

questoes.pergunta: In the hospital network's patient billing agent, first-contact resolution is 63% against an 80% target. The system prompt says only: "Escalate difficult or sensitive conversations." A review of 300 escalations finds many routine in-policy copay refunds escalated because the patient wrote angrily, while requests such as reimbursing a parking fee at an affiliated imaging center were settled by the agent on terms it made up. Which TWO changes should you make? Choose TWO.
opcoes: Replace the vague rule with explicit triggers: the patient asks for a human, the request needs an exception or is not covered by policy, or progress stalls.
Require the agent to attempt a resolution at least twice before it may escalate, so that more conversations are closed on first contact.
Add examples of borderline cases, such as an angry patient with an in-policy refund, each showing the reasoning for resolving or escalating.
Escalate requests worth more than $500 automatically, since high-value cases tend to be the complex ones that need a staff member.
Escalate when a frustration score computed from the patient's last three messages passes a set threshold, so that upset patients reach staff quickly.
questoes.explicacao: The rule "difficult or sensitive" leaves the boundary to the model, which escalates by tone and resolves policy gaps on its own. Explicit criteria plus few-shot examples of borderline cases with reasoning define when to escalate (human requested, policy exception or gap, no progress) versus resolve autonomously.
feedbacks: Correct. Explicit triggers replace the vague rule and cover the policy-gap cases the agent was resolving by invention.
This would delay patients who explicitly ask for a human and push the agent to improvise further on requests the policy does not cover.
Correct. Few-shot examples with reasoning show the model where the boundary lies in cases that look alike on the surface.
Amount is a proxy, not a trigger: the parking-fee request is small but outside policy, while many large refunds are routine and in policy.
Sentiment is an unreliable proxy for case complexity; it would keep escalating the in-policy angry patients that are hurting the resolution rate.

questoes.pergunta: In the hospital network's patient billing agent, the system prompt tells the agent to escalate "complex cases". Logs show it escalates disputes with ten or more line items that it could fully resolve with lookup_order, while in other conversations it spends 12–15 turns re-querying an insurer-status tool that keeps returning "pending" and never escalates. The team can change only the system prompt this sprint. What is the most effective fix?
opcoes: Escalate whenever a conversation passes eight turns, since long conversations are a dependable sign that the agent is stuck on a case.
Escalate when a bill has more than ten line items or exceeds $2,000, since those disputes are the ones needing specialist attention.
Escalate whenever any tool call returns an error or a pending status, so that the agent never keeps a patient waiting on a backend.
Define the triggers as a request for a human, a policy exception or gap, or no meaningful progress, not how complex a case looks.
questoes.explicacao: Complexity is the wrong trigger: the agent hands off cases it can resolve and keeps cases where it is stuck. Appropriate escalation triggers are an explicit request for a human, a policy exception or gap, and inability to make meaningful progress, and all of them can be stated in the system prompt.
feedbacks: Turn count is a crude stand-in for lack of progress: it would also escalate long but productive conversations and still miss short dead ends.
This keeps complexity as the trigger, the very thing that sends resolvable multi-line disputes to staff.
Over-escalation: a single transient error or pending status is often resolvable, and escalating on every one would sink first-contact resolution.
Correct. These are the appropriate triggers, and they correct both failure modes with a prompt-only change.

questoes.pergunta: In the hospital network's patient billing agent, each conversation starts with six to nine exploratory calls (list_policies, search_policies, list_fee_schedules) before the agent finds the refund policy or fee schedule it needs, adding about 12 seconds of latency. The MCP server that holds these documents is maintained by the same team. Which TWO changes best reduce these exploratory calls? Choose TWO.
opcoes: Load the full text of all 140 policy documents and fee schedules into the system prompt, so that the agent never has to look anything up.
Expose the index of refund and billing policy documents, with titles and section names, as an MCP resource the agent can see from the start.
Cache each conversation's exploratory results and reuse them for the next patient, so later conversations can skip the discovery calls.
Let the server publish its fee-schedule catalog, by facility and service line, as a resource the agent reads before picking a schedule.
Expose list_policies, search_policies, and list_fee_schedules as one MCP tool, discover_documents, that returns everything in a single call.
questoes.explicacao: The agent is calling tools only to learn what content exists. MCP resources expose content catalogs (here, the policy index and the fee-schedule catalog) so the agent can see what is available and fetch the right item directly, without exploratory tool calls.
feedbacks: This removes lookups by flooding every conversation with 140 documents, most irrelevant, which costs context and buries the relevant policy.
Correct. A policy index as a resource gives the agent visibility into the available documents up front.
Speculative reuse across patients risks stale or mismatched results and still pays the discovery cost whenever the cache misses.
Correct. The fee-schedule catalog as a resource lets the agent go straight to the right schedule.
Tempting because it is also exposed through MCP, but a consolidated tool still makes discovery an action the agent must call, returning a large, mostly irrelevant payload each time.

questoes.pergunta: In the hospital network's patient billing agent, a new rule says process_refund for a procedure may run only after check_claim_status confirms the insurer has not already reimbursed that procedure; skipping the check has caused several double refunds. Design 1 adds the rule to the system prompt as numbered steps with three few-shot examples. Design 2 makes the refund tool reject any call whose order ID has no check_claim_status result in the current session. Which design should you choose?
opcoes: Design 1, because numbered steps and examples let the model follow the order while still adapting when a patient's case is unusual.
Design 2, because a double refund is a financial error, and only a programmatic gate guarantees the check runs before every refund.
Design 1 plus a weekly audit of refunds, so that the rare cases in which the model skips the check are found and reversed later.
Design 2 applied to every tool in the agent, so that each conversation follows one fixed, fully predictable order of tool calls.
questoes.explicacao: When ordering errors have financial consequences, prompt guidance has a non-zero failure rate that is not acceptable. A programmatic prerequisite that blocks process_refund until check_claim_status has run for that order guarantees the sequence, while the rest of the conversation stays model-driven.
feedbacks: Prompt steps and examples raise compliance but remain probabilistic; the double refunds already show that guidance alone is not enough here.
Correct. A prerequisite gate enforces the order deterministically for the one sequence that matters.
An audit detects violations after the money has left; it does not prevent them, and reversing refunds creates its own patient problems.
Over-applied enforcement: fixing the order of every tool turns the agent into a decision tree and removes the adaptability it needs elsewhere.

questoes.pergunta: In the hospital network's patient billing agent, a send_records_link tool emails patients a download link for itemized bills and records. Compliance now requires that a link is never sent to an email address that differs from the one on file. The rule is in the system prompt today, and an audit of 4,000 calls found 3 links sent to addresses the caller typed during the chat. What should you change to meet the requirement?
opcoes: Move the rule into a dedicated compliance section of the system prompt and add two few-shot examples of declining an address the caller typed.
Add a hook that intercepts send_records_link, compares the requested address with the one on file, and blocks every call where they differ.
Add a PostToolUse hook that checks each sent link against the address on file and alerts the compliance team when the two do not match.
Remove send_records_link from the agent so that every records request is escalated to staff, who send the link after checking the address.
questoes.explicacao: The requirement says "never", which calls for a deterministic guarantee rather than better instructions. A hook that intercepts the outgoing call can compare addresses and block policy-violating calls (redirecting to staff), so compliance does not depend on the model following the prompt.
feedbacks: Better prompt structure and examples reduce violations but cannot guarantee zero; the audit already shows prompt-based compliance failing 3 times in 4,000.
Correct. Intercepting the call before it runs enforces the rule every time.
Tempting because it is also a hook, but PostToolUse runs after the link was sent; it detects the violation instead of preventing it.
This meets the rule by removing a capability the agent uses correctly 99.9% of the time, pushing all records requests to staff and lowering resolution.

questoes.pergunta: In the hospital network's patient billing agent, an intake step extracts order_number, facility, and service_date from documents that patients forward (hospital invoices, pharmacy receipts, lab statements). order_number is nullable in the schema because some messages truly lack one. It comes back null in 22% of cases, almost all of them pharmacy receipts and lab statements, yet staff find an order number in nearly every one of those documents. The prompt defines each field and includes one worked example, a hospital invoice. What is the most likely root cause?
opcoes: order_number is nullable in the schema, which lets the model return null instead of searching the document thoroughly for the value.
The extraction runs with tool_choice set to "auto", so the model sometimes answers in text and the field is lost during parsing.
The only example is a hospital invoice, so the model does not recognize how the order number appears in the other document formats.
The forwarded documents are long, and the number tends to sit in the middle of the text, where the model is least likely to notice it.
questoes.explicacao: The nulls cluster in two document formats that differ from the single example, while the value is actually present. Few-shot examples showing correct extraction from each format (how a pharmacy receipt or lab statement labels the order number) address empty extraction of fields that exist in the source.
feedbacks: Making the field nullable is correct design, since some messages lack a number; the nulls cluster by format, which points to recognition, not permission.
With "auto" and a text answer, every field would be lost for that document, not just order_number in two formats.
Correct. One example of one layout does not teach the model how other formats present the same field.
Position effects would not concentrate the failures in two document types; receipts and statements are usually short, with the number near the top.

questoes.pergunta: In the hospital network's patient billing agent, a teammate rewrote the orchestration: a classifier labels the patient's first message as one of six intents, and each intent runs a fixed tool sequence (for "refund": get_customer → lookup_order → process_refund). After launch, refunds were issued for orders that lookup_order showed as still under insurer review, and patients whose "refund" request turned out to be a billing-address problem got no help. What is the flaw in this design?
opcoes: A sequence fixed in advance stops Claude from choosing the next tool based on what the earlier tool results revealed about the case.
Six intents are too few, so the classifier should gain more intents, each with its own fixed sequence, to cover more kinds of case.
The sequences lack a prerequisite gate, so process_refund should be blocked until get_customer has returned a verified customer ID.
The classifier runs only on the first message, so it should run on each turn and switch the case to another fixed sequence as needed.
questoes.explicacao: A pre-configured decision tree executes the same steps no matter what the tools return, so it cannot react to an order under review or a request that turns out to be something else. In a model-driven loop, Claude reasons about which tool to call next based on each result, which is what these cases require.
feedbacks: Correct. The model needs to choose the next action from the results, which a fixed sequence prevents.
More intents and sequences enlarge the decision tree but keep the same flaw: no sequence can anticipate every result a tool returns.
The sequence already calls get_customer first; the failures come from ignoring what lookup_order returned, not from ordering.
Re-classifying each turn is a patch on the decision tree; it still maps cases to fixed scripts instead of reasoning from tool results.

questoes.pergunta: Scenario: Multi-Agent Research System. You are building a multi-agent research system with the Claude Agent SDK for a travel agency's product team. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: one searches the web, one analyzes documents such as supplier contracts and tourism-board studies, one synthesizes findings, and one generates the report, producing comprehensive, cited destination reports. In a report on cruise-port congestion, the search and document analysis subagents returned each claim with its source URL and excerpt, but 9 of the 31 claims in the synthesis subagent's draft have no citation or cite the wrong source. The synthesis prompt says: "Combine the findings into a coherent narrative and cite your sources." Which statement about this behavior is correct?
opcoes: Attribution broke upstream: the search subagent should have written each source into the claim text rather than attaching it separately.
The synthesis context is too small for 31 claims, so the findings should be sent in smaller groups across several synthesis calls.
Errors like these are expected when merging findings, so a fact-checking subagent should verify each claim against the web at the end.
Synthesis compresses the findings into prose without keeping the claim-source mappings, so attribution is lost as claims are merged.
questoes.explicacao: The upstream subagents delivered claim-source mappings; the attribution was lost when synthesis compressed and merged the claims into a narrative. The synthesis step must be required to preserve and merge those structured mappings (claim, source URL, excerpt) through to its output instead of relying on a generic "cite your sources".
feedbacks: Separating content from its source metadata is the right design; embedding sources in the text makes them easier to lose and harder to merge.
Batching treats a context-size problem that the symptoms do not show; each smaller synthesis call would still drop the mappings for the same reason.
Over-engineering after the fact: re-verifying every claim on the web is costly and can attach a different source than the one the finding came from.
Correct. The synthesis step must preserve and merge the claim-source mappings it receives.

questoes.pergunta: In the travel agency's research system, the web search subagent queries a government travel-advisory API. It returns an empty list both when the API times out and when there are no advisories for the destination, and the coordinator then writes "no current advisories" in the report. An engineer proposes that the subagent return a status that separates a successful query with no matches from a failed query, including the reason for the failure. How should you evaluate this proposal?
opcoes: Adopt it, so the coordinator reports "no advisories" only after a successful query and can retry or flag a gap after a failed one.
Reject it; the coordinator should treat any empty advisory result as a failure and rerun the search, since advisories affect safety.
Reject it; the subagent should retry inside its own loop until the API returns a non-empty list, so no empty result ever reaches the coordinator.
Adopt it in the logs only, so engineers can see the difference while the coordinator keeps receiving the same empty list as it does today.
questoes.explicacao: An access failure and a valid empty result mean different things: one needs a retry decision, the other is a successful answer. Reporting them distinctly lets the coordinator write "no advisories" only when that is true and retry or annotate a coverage gap when the source was unreachable.
feedbacks: Correct. Distinguishing access failures from valid empty results lets the coordinator choose the right recovery.
Treating every empty result as failure causes needless reruns for destinations that genuinely have no advisories, and still cannot tell the two cases apart.
A destination with no advisories will never return a non-empty list, so this loops on valid empty results; it also hides real outages.
Logging the distinction helps debugging, but the coordinator, which makes the recovery decision, still cannot tell a timeout from a true "none".

questoes.pergunta: In the travel agency's research system, the coordinator sends every request through all four subagents in order. Staff questions such as "What is the current visa fee for Vietnam?" take about four minutes, as long as a full market report. The team must keep the same four subagents and cannot add new services. What is the most effective fix?
opcoes: Run the same four subagents in parallel rather than in order, so staff questions finish sooner without changing which subagents run.
Have the coordinator assess what each request needs and invoke only the subagents it requires, such as web search for a single fact.
Add a classifier model in front of the coordinator that routes staff questions to a separate, lighter pipeline with its own search agent.
Cache answers to frequent staff questions and serve them directly, so the pipeline runs only for questions it has not yet answered.
questoes.explicacao: Deciding which subagents to invoke based on query complexity is part of the coordinator's role. A coordinator that analyzes the request and calls only what it needs answers a single-fact question with one subagent, without new infrastructure.
feedbacks: Parallelism does not remove unnecessary work, and synthesis and report generation depend on earlier results, so they cannot simply run alongside search.
Correct. Dynamic selection of subagents by query needs is the coordinator's job.
This adds a model and a second pipeline, which the constraint rules out, to solve what the coordinator's own decomposition should handle.
Fees and rules change, so cached answers go stale, and every new question still pays the full four-minute pipeline.

questoes.pergunta: In the travel agency's research system, the document analysis subagent calls a hotel inventory MCP tool that returns about 70 fields per property (amenities, photo URLs, 25 room types, policies). During a 20-property comparison, its context fills after a dozen calls and it starts leaving out properties it analyzed earlier, although the comparison uses only six fields. What is the most effective first step?
opcoes: Move the subagent to a model with a larger context window, so all 20 property records fit without any change to the tool results.
Trim each hotel result to the six fields the comparison uses before it is added to the subagent's context, discarding the rest.
Summarize the subagent's context after each five tool calls, so the hotel records analyzed earlier are condensed into a short paragraph.
Split the 20-property comparison across four subagents with five hotels each, and have the coordinator merge their comparisons.
questoes.explicacao: Verbose tool results accumulate in context and consume tokens far beyond their relevance. Trimming each result to the fields the task uses before it accumulates keeps all 20 properties in view at a fraction of the cost.
feedbacks: A larger window postpones the problem and still fills the context mostly with irrelevant fields that dilute attention.
Correct. Keeping only the relevant fields stops irrelevant data from accumulating.
Progressive summarization risks condensing exact rates and policies into vague text, which is precisely what a comparison needs to keep.
Over-engineering: four subagents still load 70 fields per property and add a merge step, instead of removing the irrelevant data.

questoes.pergunta: In the travel agency's research system, the web search subagent has two MCP tools: query_supplier_db ("Queries supplier data") and search_partner_catalog ("Searches partner catalog"). Both return hotel and tour information, and the wrong one is chosen in 23% of calls. Engineer A proposes rewriting both descriptions to state the data source, input formats, example queries, and when to use each instead of the other. Engineer B proposes a system-prompt rule: "If the request mentions contract, rate, or commission, use query_supplier_db." Which proposal should you choose?
opcoes: Engineer A's, because the model chooses between tools mainly from their descriptions, and these two give it nothing to tell them apart.
Engineer B's, because a keyword rule in the system prompt gives deterministic routing, unlike descriptions the model may weigh unevenly.
Engineer B's first and Engineer A's only if misrouting persists, because a prompt rule is quicker to change than tool definitions.
Neither; add a routing step before the subagent that picks the tool from the request text and removes the other tool for that call.
questoes.explicacao: Tool descriptions are the primary mechanism the model uses to select tools, and minimal descriptions make selection between similar tools unreliable. Rewriting them to state purpose, inputs, examples, and boundaries fixes the root cause; a keyword rule creates brittle associations that misfire on requests phrased differently.
feedbacks: Correct. Clear, differentiated descriptions address the root cause of misrouting.
Keyword rules are not deterministic routing; they create unintended associations (a hotel-review request that mentions "rate") and can override good descriptions.
Sequencing the keyword rule first starts with the brittle fix and leaves the actual cause, the minimal descriptions, in place.
Over-engineering: a pre-routing layer bypasses the model's understanding to solve a problem that better descriptions solve directly.

questoes.pergunta: In the travel agency's research system, the document analysis subagent receives all 18 documents for a destination (hotel contracts, local tourism regulations, insurer terms) in a single prompt. Its output covers the first contracts in depth but gives one-line notes on the last ones, and it missed that one contract's 7-day cancellation term conflicts with a local regulation requiring 14 days. The team requires consistent depth for every document and detection of conflicts between documents. What should you change?
opcoes: Move the subagent to a model with a larger context window, so all 18 documents receive full attention within the same single prompt.
Ask the subagent to fill in a fixed checklist for each document within the single prompt, so that each document gets the same fields.
Split the documents into three batches of six, analyze each batch in its own prompt, and then concatenate the three batch outputs.
Analyze each document in its own pass, then run a separate integration pass over all the extracted findings to compare terms across documents.
questoes.explicacao: Processing many documents in one pass dilutes attention, so depth drops for later documents and cross-document relationships are missed. Per-document local passes give consistent depth, and a separate integration pass compares findings across documents to catch conflicts such as the cancellation terms.
feedbacks: A larger context window does not fix attention dilution; the model can fit all 18 documents today and still treats them unevenly.
A checklist improves format consistency but keeps one diluted pass, and nothing in it compares documents with each other.
Smaller batches help depth, but with no integration step a conflict between documents in different batches is never examined.
Correct. Local passes for depth plus an integration pass for cross-document conflicts.

questoes.pergunta: In the travel agency's research system, a report on Iceland states as fact that "winter arrivals will grow 12% in 2027". Document analysis had recorded two sources: a tourism-board press release projecting 12%, and a university study projecting 3–5% whose model excludes cruise passengers. The synthesis output kept both figures with their sources, but the final report shows one number with no mention of the disagreement or of the study's method. What is the most likely root cause?
opcoes: The web search subagent found too few sources, so the report could not tell which of the two projections the evidence supported better.
Document analysis should have chosen the more credible projection, so that only one figure would have reached the later steps.
The report generator has no place for contested findings, so it flattens disputed figures and drops how each source characterized them.
The two figures sat in the middle of a long synthesis output, where the report generator was most likely to skip over the details.
questoes.explicacao: The disagreement survived until synthesis and disappeared in the report, so the report structure is the problem. Reports need explicit sections that separate well-established findings from contested ones and keep each source's characterization and methodological context, such as "projection" and "excludes cruise passengers".
feedbacks: More sources would not help if the report format still collapses disagreements into one figure; the two sources were already found.
Arbitrarily choosing one value discards credible evidence; conflicts should be annotated with attribution, not resolved by dropping a source.
Correct. Without a structure for contested findings, the generator turns a dispute into a single fact.
Position effects can cause omissions, but here the generator kept one figure and removed the qualifiers, which points to how it structures claims.

questoes.pergunta: In the travel agency's research system, for the question "Should we add Lisbon city breaks to the winter catalog?" the coordinator writes a plan of six subtasks at the start (flights, hotels, events, weather, prices, competitors) and runs exactly those. Midway, the web search subagent reports a newly announced airport tax and a planned public transport strike, but the final report mentions neither as a factor. What is the flaw in this design?
opcoes: The six subtasks ran one after another rather than in parallel, so the new findings arrived too late to reach the synthesis step.
The initial plan was too short; the coordinator should list more subtasks at the start so that topics such as taxes are included.
The plan never changes once written, so new discoveries do not lead the coordinator to create any follow-up investigation for them.
The synthesis subagent should have researched the tax and the strike itself when it saw them, instead of relying on the coordinator.
questoes.explicacao: Open-ended questions need adaptive investigation plans that generate new subtasks from intermediate findings. Here the plan was frozen at the start, so discoveries that should have triggered follow-up research were collected and then ignored.
feedbacks: Timing is not the issue; the findings did reach the coordinator midway, and nothing in the design acted on them.
A longer upfront list still cannot anticipate a tax announced during the research; the plan has to adapt to what is found.
Correct. A plan that cannot add subtasks from discoveries misses the factors that matter most.
Research belongs to the search and analysis subagents; giving synthesis that role mixes specializations instead of fixing the coordinator's planning.

questoes.pergunta: In the travel agency's research system, the document analysis subagent had two tools from different MCP servers, get_details and fetch_details, both described as "Returns details for an ID". One returns a flight itinerary by booking reference and the other a hotel property by property code, and 19% of calls used the wrong one. After the tools were renamed get_flight_itinerary and get_hotel_property and each description was rewritten with its input format and purpose, misrouting fell to 2%. Which statement about this result is correct?
opcoes: The model picks tools by name alone, so the renaming produced the whole gain and the rewritten descriptions added little to it.
The remaining 2% shows that two similar tools stay ambiguous, so they should now be merged into one get_details tool after all.
The overlapping names and descriptions caused the misrouting, and distinct names with specific descriptions removed the overlap.
The gain will hold only if the system prompt also names each tool, since tool choice depends on the prompt more than on tool definitions.
questoes.explicacao: Near-identical names and descriptions gave the model no basis to distinguish the tools. Renaming them and rewriting the descriptions around each tool's specific purpose and input eliminated the functional overlap, which is why misrouting dropped.
feedbacks: Names matter, but the model weighs the description heavily too; the change paired both, and the descriptions are what state the inputs and purpose.
Merging would reintroduce a generic tool with an unclear contract; the residual errors call for refining descriptions, not undoing the split.
Correct. Removing the overlap in names and descriptions is what fixed the selection.
The system prompt can influence selection, but the result came from the tool definitions; making it depend on prompt wording would be a step backward.

questoes.pergunta: In the travel agency's research system, an architect proposes replacing the coordinator's routing with a shared message board: each subagent posts its findings and errors there and reads what the others post, and the coordinator only collects the final report. The goal is to cut the latency of passing everything through the coordinator. How should you evaluate this proposal?
opcoes: Reject it, since routing all communication through the coordinator keeps the flow observable, handles errors consistently, and controls what each subagent receives.
Adopt it, since subagents that read each other's findings directly can build on them sooner, and the coordinator still gets the final report.
Adopt it for errors only, so a subagent that sees another subagent's failure on the board can work around it without waiting for the coordinator.
Adopt it with structured logging of every post on the board, so engineers can reconstruct the information flow whenever a report goes wrong.
questoes.explicacao: In a hub-and-spoke architecture the coordinator manages all inter-subagent communication, error handling, and information routing. A shared board removes that control point: the coordinator can no longer decide what each subagent sees, recover from errors consistently, or observe the flow while it happens.
feedbacks: Correct. Central routing is what provides observability, consistent error handling, and controlled information flow.
Lower latency is real, but subagents then act on unvetted findings and the coordinator loses the ability to steer or correct the research.
Errors are exactly what the coordinator must see to make recovery decisions; letting subagents work around each other's failures hides them.
Logs allow reconstruction after the fact, but they do not restore the coordinator's control over routing and error handling during the run.

questoes.pergunta: In the travel agency's research system, the web search subagent has 17 tools from five MCP servers (flights, hotels, weather, currency, reviews, maps, and others), although its role needs only four of them. It picks an inappropriate tool in 14% of calls, for example calling the currency converter when asked for hotel reviews. The MCP servers belong to another team and cannot be changed this quarter. What is the most effective fix?
opcoes: Ask the team that owns the MCP servers for better descriptions of the 17 tools, and add a usage table to the subagent's prompt meanwhile.
Limit the search subagent to the handful of tools its job requires, and assign the other tools to the subagents that actually use them.
Add few-shot examples to the subagent's prompt that show the right choice for each of the 17 tools, one example per tool.
Wrap the 17 tools from the five MCP servers in one travel_api tool with an operation parameter, so the subagent picks among fewer tools.
questoes.explicacao: Giving an agent many more tools than its role needs increases decision complexity and degrades selection reliability. Scoping the subagent to the four tools it actually uses removes most wrong choices immediately, and it needs no change to the MCP servers.
feedbacks: Better descriptions help, but they depend on a change that cannot happen this quarter, and 13 irrelevant tools would still crowd the choice.
Correct. Scoped tool access shrinks the choice set to what the role needs.
Seventeen examples add prompt overhead and still leave the subagent choosing among tools it should never use.
A generic wrapper hides the choice inside a parameter and loses each tool's specific contract, so misselection moves into the operation field.

questoes.pergunta: In the travel agency's research system, an analyst spent two hours with the agent building a shared baseline on Southeast Asia: sources gathered, documents analyzed, and notes on demand. She now wants to compare two report angles, budget backpackers and luxury travelers, without either line of work influencing the other and without redoing the research. What is the most effective first step?
opcoes: Fork the session twice with fork_session, so each angle starts from the same baseline in its own independent branch of the work.
Continue in the same session, asking for the budget angle first and then the luxury angle, with a reminder to keep the two separate.
Start two new sessions and rerun the research in each, so both angles are built on fresh results that are fully independent of each other.
Resume the session with --resume and ask the agent to keep the two angles in separate sections of its notes while it works on both.
questoes.explicacao: fork_session creates independent branches from a shared analysis baseline, which is exactly what comparing divergent approaches requires. Each branch inherits the research done so far, and neither branch's later reasoning leaks into the other.
feedbacks: Correct. Forking reuses the baseline and keeps the two explorations independent.
In one session the second angle is built on top of the first angle's reasoning, so the comparison is not independent.
Fresh sessions give independence but throw away two hours of valid research, which the analyst explicitly wants to avoid.
Resuming continues a single line of conversation; separate sections of notes do not stop one angle's reasoning from shaping the other.

questoes.pergunta: In the travel agency's research system, the web search subagent returns the full article text plus its own reasoning for each of about 20 sources, roughly 9,000 tokens each, and the synthesis subagent runs out of context and leaves the later sources out. Design 1 changes the upstream subagents to return structured key facts, citations, and relevance scores. Design 2 adds a step inside the synthesis subagent that summarizes each incoming result before writing. Which design should you choose?
opcoes: Design 1, because the synthesis subagent then receives only the facts and citations it needs, never the verbose content.
Design 2, because summarizing within the synthesis subagent keeps the upstream subagents simple and still shrinks what it reads.
Design 2 with a larger context window for the synthesis subagent, so it can read every result in full before it summarizes them.
Neither; let the synthesis subagent fetch each article itself when it needs details, so upstream subagents pass only the URLs.
questoes.explicacao: When the downstream agent has a limited context budget, the upstream agents should return structured data (key facts, citations, relevance scores) instead of verbose content and reasoning chains. That keeps synthesis within budget and preserves attribution, while summarizing downstream still requires loading everything first.
feedbacks: Correct. Shaping the upstream output as structured facts fits the downstream context budget.
The synthesis subagent would still have to ingest 180,000 tokens before summarizing, and its own summaries tend to drop citations and figures.
A larger window treats the symptom; synthesis still spends its attention on raw articles and reasoning it does not need.
This moves the research role into synthesis and multiplies fetches, while the verbose content still lands in its context.

questoes.pergunta: In the travel agency's research system, the report subagent runs a custom loop on the Messages API with the tools render_table and convert_currency. The code sends the request; if the response contains tool_use blocks, it executes the first one and returns that tool's output as the finished report. Reports often contain one table and none of the other sections. The requirement is that the subagent can call tools as many times as it needs before finishing. What should you change?
opcoes: Cap the loop at five iterations, so the subagent has room for several tool calls but always finishes the report within a known limit.
Execute every requested tool, append the results to the conversation, and call the model again until stop_reason is "end_turn".
Keep calling the model until the response text contains "REPORT COMPLETE", which the system prompt asks the subagent to write at the end.
Ask the model to list every tool call it will need in its first response, then run them all in order and assemble the report from the outputs.
questoes.explicacao: The agentic loop sends a request, inspects stop_reason, executes the requested tools when it is "tool_use", appends the results to the conversation, and repeats; it ends when stop_reason is "end_turn". The current code skips the return trip, so the model never sees a tool result or finishes the report.
feedbacks: An iteration cap can be a safety net, but as the main stopping rule it cuts long reports short and does not fix the missing return of results.
Correct. This is the loop lifecycle driven by stop_reason, with results returned on every iteration.
Parsing natural-language markers for termination is fragile; the model may omit or paraphrase the marker, while stop_reason is the defined signal.
Planning every call upfront turns the loop into a fixed sequence, so the model cannot choose its next step from what earlier results showed.

questoes.pergunta: In the travel agency's research system, 30% of research runs end with the coordinator restarting the whole task. Logs show that the hotel-rates API used by the web search subagent returns HTTP 503 for one or two seconds at a time; the subagent passes each 503 straight to the coordinator, which treats it as a failed subtask and starts over. A single retry after a short pause succeeds 96% of the time. What is the most likely root cause?
opcoes: The subagent escalates brief transient failures to the coordinator instead of retrying locally and escalating only what it cannot resolve.
The coordinator splits the research into too many dependent subtasks, so a failure in any one of them invalidates the whole run.
The hotel-rates tool's description does not warn about 503 responses, so the subagent cannot plan around them when choosing tools.
The error passed to the coordinator lacks structured context such as partial results, so the coordinator has no basis to continue.
questoes.explicacao: Transient failures that a short retry would fix should be handled inside the subagent. Only errors it cannot resolve locally should reach the coordinator, together with what was attempted and any partial results, so the coordinator is not pulled into routine recovery.
feedbacks: Correct. Local recovery for transient failures keeps routine blips from reaching the coordinator.
Decomposition shape does not explain the trigger: the restarts follow brief, recoverable 503s that never needed to leave the subagent.
Tool descriptions guide selection, not failure handling; no description would stop a 503 from occurring or decide when to retry it.
Partial results matter when an error truly must be escalated, but these errors should not have been escalated at all.

questoes.pergunta: Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude. You are building developer productivity tools with the Claude Agent SDK at a cybersecurity vendor whose engineers maintain a 12-year-old threat-detection platform. The agent helps engineers explore unfamiliar codebases, understand legacy systems, generate boilerplate code, and automate repetitive tasks, using the built-in tools (Read, Write, Bash, Grep, Glob) and MCP servers for the internal vulnerability database and ticket tracker. While building it, the team also uses Claude Code directly. One engineer is spending a week investigating the legacy license-enforcement module in Claude Code: each morning she starts a new session and spends about 25 minutes re-exploring code that was already analyzed, and on Wednesday two teammates merged changes to three files in that module. Which TWO practices should she adopt? Choose TWO.
opcoes: When resuming after the merges, tell Claude which three files changed and ask it to re-analyze them, rather than re-exploring the module.
Paste the full transcript of the previous day's session into the first prompt of a new session, so nothing from the earlier analysis is lost.
Start each morning with fork_session from Monday's session, so each day's work runs in its own branch separate from the earlier analysis.
Give the investigation a session name and continue it each morning with --resume and that name, instead of starting a new session.
Record the investigation's findings in the repository's CLAUDE.md, so that each session in the repository starts with them already loaded.
questoes.explicacao: Named session resumption with --resume <session-name> continues a specific investigation with its prior context instead of rebuilding it each day. When files changed since the last session, telling the resumed session exactly which ones changed allows targeted re-analysis rather than full re-exploration.
feedbacks: Correct. Informing the resumed session about the specific changed files avoids stale conclusions without a full re-exploration.
A pasted transcript is bulky, loses the structure of the original session, and fills the new context with raw history instead of resuming it.
fork_session is for exploring divergent approaches from a shared baseline; daily forks scatter one linear investigation across branches.
Correct. Naming the session and resuming it by name continues the investigation across days.
CLAUDE.md is shared, always-loaded project configuration; one engineer's in-progress notes would load into every teammate's sessions.

questoes.pergunta: At the cybersecurity vendor, engineers use Claude Code in the detection-platform repository while building the agent. Three observations: an instruction Priya added to ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md ("run make lint-sec before proposing a commit") is followed in her sessions but not in her teammates'; the conventions in the repository's root CLAUDE.md are followed by everyone; and the rules in sensors/CLAUDE.md are applied only when Claude works on files under sensors/. Which statement correctly explains these observations?
opcoes: The root CLAUDE.md overrides user-level files for everyone except their author, and sensors/CLAUDE.md loads only if the root file imports it.
User-level files apply only to their user, the project file is shared through version control, and a directory file applies to its subtree.
Teammates lack Priya's instruction because user-level files sync only after each person runs /memory, while project files load at startup.
All three files are shared through the repository, but user-level instructions apply only to commit actions, so teammates rarely trigger it.
questoes.explicacao: CLAUDE.md has three levels: user-level (~/.claude/CLAUDE.md) applies only to that user and is not shared through version control; project-level (root CLAUDE.md or .claude/CLAUDE.md) is shared with everyone who clones the repository; directory-level files apply when working in that subdirectory. Each observation matches one level.
feedbacks: There is no override-except-author rule, and a subdirectory CLAUDE.md does not need to be imported to apply to its own directory.
Correct. This is the user, project, and directory hierarchy, and each observation follows from it.
/memory shows and edits the memory files that are loaded; it does not sync anything between users, and a file in Priya's home directory never reaches her teammates.
~/.claude/CLAUDE.md lives in Priya's home directory and is not in the repository at all, so it cannot be shared with teammates.

questoes.pergunta: At the cybersecurity vendor, the team's /triage-cve skill (.claude/skills/triage-cve/SKILL.md) needs a CVE identifier and the affected product version. Engineers often invoke it with no arguments; the skill then guesses the version from the latest release tag and produces wrong triage notes in about one run in five. An engineer proposes adding argument-hint: "<cve-id> <product-version>" to the skill's frontmatter. How should you evaluate this proposal?
opcoes: Adopt it, because argument-hint shows engineers which parameters the skill expects when they invoke it, so they supply both values.
Reject it; put the parameter requirement in the root CLAUDE.md instead, so it is always in context when an engineer invokes the skill.
Reject it; add context: fork instead, so that the skill runs in an isolated subagent that can stop and ask for any missing value.
Reject it; split the skill into two skills that each take one parameter, so engineers cannot invoke either one without its value.
questoes.explicacao: argument-hint is the SKILL.md frontmatter option for prompting developers about required parameters when they invoke a skill. Showing "<cve-id> <product-version>" at invocation time addresses the missing-argument runs directly, at the point where the engineer types the command.
feedbacks: Correct. argument-hint is designed to prompt for the skill's required parameters.
CLAUDE.md holds always-loaded universal standards; a requirement specific to one skill does not belong there and is not shown when the command is typed.
context: fork isolates verbose or exploratory skill output from the main session; it does not make the skill collect missing arguments.
Two skills fragment one workflow and still do not stop an engineer from invoking either skill without its argument.

questoes.pergunta: At the cybersecurity vendor, the agent's boilerplate task must set enabled: true for the dns-tunnel detector in detectors.yaml. The file has seven detector blocks generated from one template, with hand-tuned thresholds in several of them, so the lines around enabled: false are identical in every block. Edit fails because the text to replace is not unique, and the run must finish without a person editing the file. What is the most effective fix?
opcoes: Retry Edit with replace_all enabled, so that the tool accepts the non-unique text and changes the enabled line in the file.
Read the full file, change the enabled line inside the dns-tunnel block in that content, and Write the complete file back.
Use Bash with sed to replace the first enabled: false in the file, since detector blocks are listed in alphabetical order.
Regenerate detectors.yaml from the template with Write, so that each block is rebuilt with dns-tunnel set to enabled: true.
questoes.explicacao: Edit needs a unique anchor, and here it has none. The documented fallback is to Read the whole file, make the change in the loaded content where the dns-tunnel block can be located unambiguously, and Write the full file back, which modifies exactly one block and keeps the hand-tuned values.
feedbacks: replace_all would enable all seven detectors, not just dns-tunnel, which is a different and harmful change.
Correct. Read + Write is the reliable fallback when Edit cannot find unique anchor text.
This relies on an assumption about file order that nothing guarantees; if dns-tunnel is not first, the wrong detector is enabled.
Rebuilding from the template overwrites the hand-tuned thresholds in the other blocks; Write without reading first loses existing content.

questoes.pergunta: At the cybersecurity vendor, the agent is preparing a migration report. It must list every YARA detection-rule file (named *.yara and spread across about 40 directories) and every versioned database migration script under db/migrations/ (named like V112__add_index.sql). Which TWO tool selections are correct? Choose TWO.
opcoes: Grep with the pattern \.yara across the repository to find which of the files are detection rules.
Read on each directory under rules/ to discover the detection-rule files one directory at a time.
Grep with the pattern V[0-9]+__ to locate the migration scripts by the version prefix they use.
Glob with the pattern db/migrations/V*__*.sql to list the versioned migration scripts by name.
Glob with the pattern **/*.yara to list every detection-rule file, whatever directory it is stored in.
questoes.explicacao: Both needs are about file names, not file contents, so Glob is the right tool: **/*.yara matches the rule files in any directory, and db/migrations/V*__*.sql matches the versioned scripts. Grep searches inside files, so it finds references to these names rather than the files themselves.
feedbacks: Grep searches file contents, so it returns files that mention ".yara" (build scripts, docs) and misses rule files that never mention their own extension.
Read loads file contents; walking directories with it is slow, and the files may live outside rules/ anyway.
This matches the version prefix inside file contents, such as references in a changelog, not the script file names.
Correct. A Glob pattern on the path finds the migration scripts by their naming convention.
Correct. Glob matches file paths by pattern, regardless of directory depth.

questoes.pergunta: At the cybersecurity vendor, engineers report that Claude Code follows the team's secure-coding conventions in some sessions in the detection-platform repository but ignores them in others. The conventions are spread across the root CLAUDE.md, an @import of docs/secure-coding.md, and several directory-level CLAUDE.md files. One engineer wants to merge everything into the root CLAUDE.md right away; another wants to diagnose the problem first. What should you do?
opcoes: Merge everything into the root CLAUDE.md now, since a single file guarantees that each session loads the same set of instructions.
Ask Claude at the start of an affected session which instructions it is following, and compare its answer with the convention files.
Copy the conventions into every directory-level CLAUDE.md, so that sessions started from any directory load the complete set of rules.
Run /memory in a session that ignores the conventions and in one that follows them, and compare which memory files each session loaded.
questoes.explicacao: Inconsistent behavior across sessions usually means different memory files are loaded, for example depending on the directory or a broken import. /memory shows which memory files a session has loaded, so comparing a failing and a working session identifies the cause before anyone restructures the configuration.
feedbacks: Consolidating may hide the symptom, but without a diagnosis it can also break directory-specific rules and leaves the real cause (such as a bad import path) unknown.
The model's description of its own instructions is not a reliable record of which files were loaded; /memory shows that directly.
Duplicating rules into every directory creates copies that drift and still does not explain why some sessions miss them.
Correct. /memory verifies which memory files are loaded, which is the diagnostic for inconsistent behavior.

questoes.pergunta: At the cybersecurity vendor, the /map-legacy-module skill (.claude/skills/map-legacy-module/SKILL.md) walks a module and produces about 3,000 lines of discovery output that then remain in the engineer's main conversation. The security team also requires that this skill can only read and search files, never write them or run shell commands. What should you change in the skill?
opcoes: Move the skill to .claude/commands/map-legacy-module.md, so that it runs as a slash command and keeps its output out of the conversation.
Add instructions to the SKILL.md body to keep the output under 50 lines and never to write files or run Bash during the module walk.
Add allowed-tools: Read, Grep, Glob to the frontmatter, and ask engineers to run /compact after each use to clear the long output.
Add context: fork and allowed-tools: Read, Grep, Glob to the SKILL.md frontmatter, so the skill runs isolated and with read-only tools.
questoes.explicacao: SKILL.md frontmatter supports context: fork, which runs the skill in an isolated sub-agent context so its verbose output does not pollute the main conversation, and allowed-tools, which restricts the tools available while the skill runs. Together they meet both requirements.
feedbacks: Moving it to commands changes how it is stored, not where it runs; the output would still land in the main conversation.
Prompt instructions are not a restriction: the skill could still write files or run Bash, and a 50-line cap would cut the analysis short.
allowed-tools covers the security requirement, but relying on engineers to run /compact each time is a manual workaround for what context: fork does.
Correct. context: fork isolates the output, and allowed-tools limits the skill to read-only tools.

questoes.pergunta: At the cybersecurity vendor, the agent defines a dependency-auditor subagent with an AgentDefinition whose description says "Audits third-party dependencies for known CVEs" and whose system prompt says "You are read-only; never modify files." The definition has no tools field. During an audit, the subagent ran git checkout on a lockfile and then edited it. What is the most likely root cause?
opcoes: The coordinator's allowedTools does not include "Task", so the subagent ran with the coordinator's tool set, not its AgentDefinition's.
With no tool restrictions in its definition, the auditor inherited the full tool set, and only its prompt stood in the way of edits.
The subagent inherited the coordinator's conversation, in which an engineer had asked the agent earlier to update the lockfile.
The AgentDefinition's description is too vague, so the coordinator sent a lockfile update to the auditor instead of the edit subagent.
questoes.explicacao: An AgentDefinition configures a subagent's description, system prompt, and tool restrictions. Without a tools restriction the subagent has the full tool set, so "read-only" depends entirely on prompt compliance; restricting it to read and search tools makes the boundary enforceable.
feedbacks: Without "Task" in allowedTools the coordinator could not have spawned the subagent at all, yet the log shows it running.
Correct. The missing tool restriction left the read-only rule to the prompt alone.
Subagents do not inherit the coordinator's conversation history; they see only what is passed in their prompt.
The description is specific to auditing, and the subagent was invoked for an audit; the problem is what it could do, not why it was chosen.

questoes.pergunta: At the cybersecurity vendor, a job maps a two-million-line legacy codebase. The coordinator spawns one subagent per module; each subagent writes its findings to state/<module>.json after every directory it finishes, and the coordinator keeps a manifest of completed modules. After a crash, the coordinator loads the manifest, skips completed modules, and respawns the unfinished subagents with their original task prompts. Unfinished modules are then re-mapped from the beginning. What is the flaw?
opcoes: Subagents should write their state only when a module is complete, since partial files make it unclear which findings can be trusted.
On resume, the respawned subagents' prompts omit their modules' saved state, so each one redoes work it had already recorded.
The manifest should live in the coordinator's conversation history rather than on disk, so that it is restored along with the session.
Each subagent should keep its findings in its own context and return them only at the end, so the coordinator has one source of truth.
questoes.explicacao: Crash recovery works when each agent exports its state to a known location and the coordinator loads the manifest on resume and injects that state into the agents' prompts. Here the state is saved and the manifest is read, but the partial state is never handed back to the respawned subagents.
feedbacks: Writing only at completion would lose all progress on a crash, which is the opposite of what incremental state exports are for.
Correct. The saved state must be injected into the respawned agent's prompt for the recovery to resume work.
A crash can lose the conversation itself; state on disk at a known location is what survives and can be reloaded.
Keeping findings only in context means a crash loses them entirely, removing the recovery mechanism instead of fixing it.

questoes.pergunta: At the cybersecurity vendor, a reviewer inspects an agent run that scaffolded a new detector: it used Write to create detectors/dns_tunnel.py (180 new lines) and Edit to change one import line in detectors/__init__.py. The reviewer asks whether the agent should have used Write for both files, for consistency. Which statement is correct?
opcoes: Write suits creating or fully replacing a file, while Edit suits a targeted change matched on unique text without rewriting the rest.
Write should be used for both, because Edit is only a fallback for when Write fails and is less dependable for existing files.
Edit should be used for both, because creating a file through Edit checks the new content against the project's existing structure.
Either choice is equivalent here, because both tools rewrite the whole file on disk and differ only in how the change is expressed.
questoes.explicacao: Read and Write handle full-file operations, so Write fits a new file. Edit performs targeted modifications by matching unique text, so it fits a one-line change in an existing file without regenerating, and possibly altering, the rest of it.
feedbacks: Correct. Each tool was used for the job it is designed for.
This reverses the relationship: Read + Write is the fallback when Edit cannot find a unique match, not the other way round.
Edit performs no such check; it replaces matched text in an existing file and is not the tool for creating new files.
The difference is not cosmetic: rewriting a whole file to change one line risks altering content the agent did not mean to touch.

questoes.pergunta: At the cybersecurity vendor, an engineer with no background in threat-intelligence feeds must build a local cache for the indicator lookups that the agent makes through MCP. Her lead proposes that, before any code is written, she ask Claude to interview her about the requirements instead of giving it a one-line request. How should you evaluate this proposal?
opcoes: Reject it; she should write a detailed specification on her own first, since Claude can only implement what has been fully specified.
Adopt it, since Claude's questions can raise issues she may not foresee, such as invalidating revoked indicators and handling a feed outage.
Reject it; she should build a first version and iterate by sharing test failures, since tests expose missing requirements more quickly.
Adopt it, but limit Claude to yes-or-no questions, so that the interview stays short and she keeps control of the design decisions.
questoes.explicacao: In an unfamiliar domain, the interview pattern has Claude ask questions that surface design considerations the developer may not anticipate, such as cache invalidation and failure modes, before implementation. That prevents building on wrong assumptions.
feedbacks: She lacks the domain knowledge to write a complete specification alone; the interview is how the missing considerations come out.
Correct. The interview pattern surfaces considerations such as invalidation and failure modes before implementing.
Test-driven iteration works when the expected behavior is known; here she does not yet know which behaviors the tests should cover.
Yes-or-no questions can only confirm what she already thought of, which defeats the purpose of surfacing unanticipated issues.

questoes.pergunta: At the cybersecurity vendor, an engineer asks the agent how an alert flows from the sensor to the analyst dashboard across four services. The agent runs dozens of Grep and Read calls in its own context; after about 90,000 tokens of file contents it starts mixing up class names between services and loses track of the original question. The engineer must keep working in this one conversation. What is the most effective fix?
opcoes: Move the agent to a model with a larger context window, so that all four services' file contents fit before it starts to lose track.
Tell the agent to read only the first 100 lines of each file, so that its discovery output stays small enough to fit in its context.
Have the agent save each file it reads to a scratchpad file and re-read that file whenever it needs to recall a detail from a service.
Have the agent delegate each service's exploration to a subagent that returns a concise summary for the main agent to use.
questoes.explicacao: Verbose exploration output degrades the main context.
