Delegating each service's exploration to a subagent isolates the raw file contents in the subagent's context, and the main agent receives concise summaries it can use to coordinate the end-to-end answer within the same conversation.
feedbacks: A larger window delays the degradation, but the context still fills with raw file contents that dilute attention to the question.
Truncating files hides the parts that often matter, such as handlers further down a file, so the trace becomes incomplete.
A scratchpad should hold key findings, not raw file copies; re-reading full files brings the same verbose content back into context.
Correct. Subagents isolate verbose exploration while the main agent keeps the high-level picture.

questoes.pergunta: At the cybersecurity vendor, an engineer uses Claude Code for a multi-phase task: find every place in nine services where the legacy license check is called or configured, then design and implement its replacement. During the first phase the main conversation fills with search output, and the session runs low on context before any design work starts. Which TWO changes should the engineer make? Choose TWO.
opcoes: Ask Claude to print shorter search results during discovery, so that each Grep and Read call adds less output to the conversation.
Run the discovery phase in the Explore subagent, so that the verbose search output stays isolated and only a summary comes back.
Carry the summary of discovery findings into the design phase as its starting context, instead of the raw search output itself.
Split the nine services across nine separate Claude Code sessions, and merge their notes by hand before starting the design work.
Run discovery in the main session and use /clear before the design phase, so that the design work starts with a fresh context window.
questoes.explicacao: The Explore subagent isolates verbose discovery output and returns a summary, preserving the main conversation's context for later phases. Starting the design phase from that summary of findings, rather than raw output, keeps the important results while avoiding context exhaustion.
feedbacks: Shorter printing loses details without isolating anything; the search work still accumulates in the main conversation.
Correct. The Explore subagent keeps verbose discovery out of the main context and returns a summary.
Correct. Injecting a summary of the previous phase's findings carries forward what matters without the verbose output.
Nine sessions plus manual merging shifts coordination work to the engineer and loses cross-service connections.
/clear frees the context but discards the discovery findings the design phase needs.

questoes.pergunta: At the cybersecurity vendor, the team must replace a homegrown cryptography wrapper used in 38 files with the standard library's API. Some call sites rely on the wrapper silently falling back to an older cipher, and nobody knows how many. One engineer wants to start editing right away to save time; another wants to use plan mode. Which approach should the team take?
opcoes: Start editing right away in direct execution, with a detailed instruction on the standard library's API, so all 38 files change in one run.
Start editing three call sites in direct execution, then extend the same change to the wrapper's other call sites once they pass tests.
Stay in plan mode for the whole task, so that every file change is reviewed as a plan before Claude writes anything to the disk.
Use plan mode to explore the call sites and design the migration before editing, then switch to direct execution for the planned changes.
questoes.explicacao: Plan mode lets Claude explore the codebase and design the approach before committing to changes, which prevents costly rework when hidden dependencies, such as the silent cipher fallback, turn up late. Once the plan is settled, direct execution implements it efficiently.
feedbacks: A uniform instruction assumes every call site is the same, which is exactly what is unknown; fallback-dependent sites would break.
Three sample call sites may not include any that depend on the fallback, so the pattern can look safe until it fails elsewhere.
Plan mode is for exploring and designing; implementation still has to happen, and staying in it does not carry out the migration.
Correct. Plan first to surface the unknowns, then execute the planned changes directly.

questoes.pergunta: At the cybersecurity vendor, the agent converts legacy detection rules from an INI-style format to the new YAML schema. The instruction says, in prose, to "map the old severity levels to the new scale and merge duplicate tags". Reviewers find that about 30% of outputs map severities differently from one run to the next, and some drop tags instead of merging them. What should you change?
opcoes: Expand the prose instruction with a paragraph on each severity level and on what counts as a duplicate tag, so the rules are unambiguous.
Add a programmatic schema check on the YAML output, so that malformed rules are caught and the conversion is retried until it passes.
Add two or three concrete examples, each showing a legacy rule and its exact expected YAML output, including one with merged tags.
Ask Claude to restate its understanding of the mapping before each run, so that the engineer can correct it before rules are written.
questoes.explicacao: When prose descriptions of a transformation are interpreted inconsistently, concrete input/output examples are the most effective way to communicate it. Two or three examples that show the exact mapping and a tag merge pin down the behavior that the prose left open.
feedbacks: More prose adds detail, but the problem is that prose is being interpreted inconsistently; longer prose leaves the same room for interpretation.
A schema check catches structural errors, but a wrong severity or a dropped tag can be perfectly valid against the schema.
Correct. Concrete input/output examples remove the ambiguity that the prose leaves.
A restated understanding adds a manual review step to every run and still leaves the mapping defined only in prose.

questoes.pergunta: Scenario: Claude Code for Continuous Integration. You are integrating Claude Code into the CI/CD pipeline of an automotive manufacturer's software division, which builds firmware for electronic control units (ECUs) and an infotainment app. The pipeline runs automated code reviews, generates test cases, and posts feedback on pull requests, and its prompts must give actionable feedback while minimizing false positives. One test-planning step calls the Messages API directly with a tool named record_test_cases whose input_schema defines the test fields, and tool_choice forces that tool. The parser reads response.content[0].text and reports "0 test cases" on nearly every run, although the logged responses contain complete test data. What is the most likely root cause?
opcoes: The input_schema marks too few fields as required, so the model returns partial test cases that the parser discards as invalid.
Forcing the tool stops the model from writing explanatory text, so tool_choice should be "auto" to get both text and test data.
The test data arrives as the input of the tool_use block, so the parser must read that block's input instead of a text block.
max_tokens is too low for the test list, so the response is cut off before the text block holding the test cases is written.
questoes.explicacao: With a tool whose input_schema defines the output, the structured data comes back as the input of a tool_use content block, not as text. The parser must locate the tool_use block for record_test_cases and read its input; there is no text block to parse when the tool is forced.
feedbacks: Required fields affect completeness, but the logs show complete data; the parser never looks at where that data is.
Switching to "auto" would allow the model to skip the tool and answer in free text, giving up the guaranteed structure.
Correct. Structured output from tool use is extracted from the tool_use block's input.
Truncation would show stop_reason "max_tokens" and partial data, not complete test data in every logged response.

questoes.pergunta: In the automotive manufacturer's CI pipeline, a job runs claude -p "Review this diff against our ECU coding rules" and a script parses the free-text answer to post inline PR comments. About 6% of runs break the parser because file paths, line numbers, or severities appear in unexpected places. Which TWO changes make the findings reliably machine-parseable? Choose TWO.
opcoes: Post-process the text with stricter regular expressions for path:line patterns and drop findings that do not match.
Pass --json-schema with a schema defining file, line, severity, and message, so the findings follow that structure.
Run the job with --output-format json, so that Claude Code returns its result as JSON instead of as plain text output.
Add an explicit instruction to respond only with JSON containing file, line, severity, and message, and keep parsing the text.
Send the free-text review to a second Claude call that rewrites it as JSON before the comment-posting script runs.
questoes.explicacao: In CI, --output-format json makes Claude Code emit machine-readable output, and --json-schema enforces the shape of the findings (file, line, severity, message). Together they produce structured findings that a script can post as inline PR comments without fragile text parsing.
feedbacks: Stricter regexes make parsing pickier and silently drop real findings, without making the output itself structured.
Correct. The schema fixes the structure of each finding for automated posting.
Correct. JSON output format makes the result machine-readable.
A prompt instruction raises the odds of JSON but does not enforce it, so the parser keeps failing on some runs.
A second call adds cost and latency and can itself drift; the CLI flags give structured output directly.

questoes.pergunta: In the automotive manufacturer's CI pipeline, developers dismiss 40% of the automated review comments on the infotainment app. The team wants to learn which kinds of findings get dismissed so that it can tune the review prompt systematically. Today each finding has file, line, severity, and message fields. Which TWO changes best support this analysis? Choose TWO.
opcoes: Add a detected_pattern field to each finding that names the code construct that triggered it, such as an unchecked cast.
Record which posted findings developers dismiss, and compute dismissal rates per triggering code construct to find the noisy ones.
Require developers to type a reason each time they dismiss a comment, so the team can read through the reasons each month.
Ask the model to attach a confidence score to each finding and stop posting findings below 0.7, so fewer comments get dismissed.
Have Claude re-review each dismissed finding in a later run to decide whether the developer or the original review was right.
questoes.explicacao: A detected_pattern field records which code construct triggered each finding. Joining that with recorded dismissal outcomes shows which patterns produce false positives, so prompt changes can target those patterns instead of guessing.
feedbacks: Correct. detected_pattern tags each finding with the construct that triggered it.
Correct. Dismissal rates per triggering construct reveal the systematic false-positive sources to target in the prompt.
Free-text reasons depend on developer diligence and are hard to aggregate; they do not tie the dismissal to the construct that caused it.
Confidence filtering hides findings without explaining which kinds are wrong, and the model can be confident about the noisy patterns too.
A model judging past disputes adds cost and does not produce the per-pattern statistics needed to tune the prompt.

questoes.pergunta: In the automotive manufacturer's CI pipeline, the root CLAUDE.md holds 600 lines of ECU C conventions that load for every job, including reviews of the infotainment app's Kotlin code. An engineer proposes moving them to .claude/rules/ecu-c.md with YAML frontmatter paths: ["ecu/**/*.c", "ecu/**/*.h"]. How should you evaluate this proposal?
opcoes: Adopt it, because a rule file with a paths glob loads only when Claude works on matching files, keeping ECU rules out of Kotlin reviews.
Reject it, because every file in .claude/rules/ is loaded at startup regardless of its frontmatter, so the context would not shrink at all.
Reject it, and turn the conventions into a skill that the CI job invokes for ECU pull requests, so that they load only on demand.
Reject it, because path-scoped rules load only in interactive sessions, so CI jobs started with -p would never receive the conventions.
questoes.explicacao: Rule files in .claude/rules/ with a paths field in YAML frontmatter activate only when Claude edits or reads files matching the glob. Moving the ECU conventions there keeps them available for ECU work and removes them from every unrelated job, reducing irrelevant context and token usage.
feedbacks: Correct. Path-scoped rules load conditionally on matching files.
The paths frontmatter exists precisely to make loading conditional; only rule files without it load unconditionally.
A skill depends on being invoked, so a CI job or developer that forgets loses the conventions; path rules apply automatically by file.
Path-scoped rules are part of the project configuration that Claude Code loads in -p runs as well; they apply whenever matching files are touched.

questoes.pergunta: In the automotive manufacturer's CI pipeline, the review posts findings in four categories: memory safety, concurrency, naming, and documentation. The documentation category has a 70% false positive rate, and developers have started dismissing all review comments unread, including accurate memory-safety findings. Rewriting the documentation criteria will take about three weeks, and trust must be restored now. What is the most effective fix?
opcoes: Disable the documentation category for now while its criteria are rewritten, and keep posting the categories that are already precise.
Keep all four categories but post documentation findings at an informational level, so that developers can tell them apart from others.
Add "only report findings you are highly confident about" to the review prompt, so that the weaker documentation findings are dropped.
Run the review twice and post only findings that appear in both runs, so that inconsistent documentation findings are removed automatically.
questoes.explicacao: A category with a high false-positive rate undermines trust in the accurate categories too, which is why developers now ignore memory-safety findings. Temporarily disabling the noisy category restores trust immediately, while its criteria are improved before it is turned back on.
feedbacks: Correct. Temporarily disabling the high false-positive category protects trust in the precise ones.
Relabeling keeps the noisy comments in front of developers, so the habit of dismissing everything continues.
Vague confidence instructions do not improve precision; the documentation findings are often confidently wrong.
Consensus filtering can drop real but intermittent findings and doubles cost, without addressing the flawed documentation criteria.

questoes.pergunta: In the automotive manufacturer's CI pipeline, nightly test generation for merged changes is moving to the Message Batches API for its 50% cost savings. A batch can take up to 24 hours to process. The quality team's SLA says generated tests must be available within 36 hours of a merge. Merges arrive throughout the day and wait in a queue until the next submission. Which submission schedule guarantees the SLA while keeping batch pricing?
opcoes: Submit every 24 hours, so each batch finishes before the next one is sent and the queue never holds more than a day of merges.
Submit every 8 hours, so a merge waits at most 8 hours plus up to 24 of processing, leaving a 4-hour margin under the SLA.
Submit every 16 hours, so a merge waits at most 16 hours plus up to 24 of processing, which spreads the load over fewer batches.
Submit whenever 10,000 merges have accumulated, so that each batch is large enough to make the most of the batch discount.
questoes.explicacao: The worst case is a merge that arrives just after a submission: it waits one full interval and then up to 24 hours of processing. Every 8 hours gives 8 + 24 = 32 hours, inside the 36-hour SLA with a 4-hour operational margin (for example, for a delayed submission), the same logic as using 4-hour windows to guarantee a 30-hour SLA; 16 or 24 hours exceed the SLA in the worst case.
feedbacks: Tempting because batches never overlap, but a merge that arrives just after a submission waits 24 hours and may need 24 more: 48 hours, past the 36-hour SLA.
Correct. The worst case is 8 + 24 = 32 hours, which meets the 36-hour SLA with a 4-hour operational margin.
Fewer batches is appealing, but the worst case is 16 + 24 = 40 hours, which breaks the 36-hour SLA.
A count-based trigger makes the queue wait unbounded on quiet days, so no completion time can be guaranteed; the schedule has to be time-based.

questoes.pergunta: In the automotive manufacturer's CI pipeline, a single review pass covers a 22-file pull request to the battery-management firmware. Comments thin out toward the end of the diff: the last eight files got none, although a later audit found three defects there. The review also missed that a signal's unit changed from millivolts to volts in a producer file but not in its consumer, which lives in another directory. Which review design best addresses both problems?
opcoes: Review each file in its own pass, run those passes in parallel, and merge the per-file comments into a single review for the PR.
Keep the single pass but move it to a model with a larger context window, so all 22 files and their relationships fit at once.
Review each file in its own pass for local issues, then run a separate integration pass over the changes for cross-file data flow.
Group the files by directory into four chunks and review each chunk in one pass, so that related files are analyzed together.
questoes.explicacao: Reviewing many files in one pass dilutes attention, so later files get shallow treatment. Per-file passes give each file full attention for local issues, and a separate integration pass examines data flow across files, such as the producer and consumer that disagree on units.
feedbacks: Per-file passes fix the depth problem, but without an integration pass no step ever compares the producer with its consumer.
A larger context window does not fix attention dilution; the files already fit, and the depth still falls off.
Correct. Local passes plus a cross-file integration pass address both the dilution and the cross-file defect.
Chunking by directory helps depth but splits the producer and consumer into different chunks, so the unit mismatch is still missed.

questoes.pergunta: In the automotive manufacturer's CI pipeline, a step generates structured test specifications for each changed CAN-bus handler, and a Pydantic validator rejects 9% of them, for example when expected_value falls outside the signal's declared range or a fixture name does not exist. On failure, the job resends the identical prompt up to three times, and only 20% of the retries pass. What should you change?
opcoes: Raise the retry limit from three to six attempts, since each additional attempt has another chance of producing a specification that passes.
Send failed items to a larger model on retry, since validation failures suggest the task is too hard for the model of the first attempt.
Relax the validator to log range and fixture problems as warnings, so the job stops failing on issues that reviewers can catch later.
On retry, send the original input, the failed specification, and the specific validation errors, so the model can correct those fields.
questoes.explicacao: An identical prompt gives the model no information about what was wrong, so retries mostly repeat the mistake. Retry-with-error-feedback appends the specific validation errors, along with the original input and the failed output, so the model can correct the offending fields.
feedbacks: More identical retries repeat the same blind attempt; without the error details the success rate per retry stays low.
A larger model also lacks the validator's feedback, and the errors (out-of-range value, unknown fixture) are specific and correctable.
Downgrading errors to warnings lets invalid tests into the pipeline and moves the problem to reviewers instead of fixing it.
Correct. Feeding back the specific validation errors guides the model to a correct specification.

questoes.pergunta: In the automotive manufacturer's CI pipeline, a job runs Claude Code with -p to generate unit tests for changed ECU modules. The generated tests build raw mocks instead of using the team's can_bus_fixture helpers and skip the boundary cases the team requires. Developers who use Claude Code locally get conforming tests because they usually begin with "follow docs/testing.md". The repository's CLAUDE.md contains only build commands. What is the most likely root cause?
opcoes: The standards live in a document developers mention by hand, and the CLAUDE.md that CI-invoked Claude Code loads does not include them.
Claude Code does not load CLAUDE.md files when it runs with -p, so CI jobs can receive conventions only through the prompt text.
The job does not use --output-format json, so Claude Code treats the request as free text and ignores the repository's conventions.
The -p job starts each run in a fresh session, while developers' local sessions keep the testing conventions from earlier conversations.
questoes.explicacao: CLAUDE.md is the mechanism for giving CI-invoked Claude Code project context such as testing standards, fixture conventions, and review criteria. Here the conventions exist only in a document that developers mention by hand, so the CI job never sees them; documenting or importing them in the project CLAUDE.md fixes that.
feedbacks: Correct. The CI job's project context comes from CLAUDE.md, which lacks the testing standards.
CLAUDE.md is loaded in -p runs as well; that is why it is the recommended place for CI context.
Output format controls how results are returned, not which project conventions the model follows.
Tempting because the local sessions do behave differently, but the difference is the instruction developers type; the conventions belong in versioned project context that every run loads.

questoes.pergunta: In the automotive manufacturer's CI pipeline, review findings are produced through a tool whose schema defines category as an enum of memory_safety, concurrency, misra_violation, and style, and marks every field as required, including misra_rule_id and suggested_fix. Reviewers notice that findings about deprecated APIs are labeled style, and that findings unrelated to MISRA carry rule IDs such as "Rule 21.99", which does not exist. What is the flaw in this schema?
opcoes: The category enum has too many values, so memory_safety, concurrency, misra_violation, and style should become two broad categories.
category should be a free-text string, so that the model can describe each finding in its own words instead of choosing from a list.
misra_rule_id is required although many findings have no rule, and the enum lacks an "other" value with a detail field for new kinds.
Enforcing the schema through tool use constrains the model too much, and asking for JSON in the prompt would give more accurate fields.
questoes.explicacao: A required field forces the model to supply a value even when the source has none, which invites fabrication; misra_rule_id should be optional or nullable. A closed enum with no "other" option forces findings into the nearest wrong category; adding "other" plus a detail string keeps the categorization extensible.
feedbacks: Fewer categories make the labels less useful and still force findings into categories that do not fit them.
Free text loses the structure that downstream tooling relies on; an "other" value with a detail field keeps both.
Correct. Required fields without a source value and closed enums without "other" cause both observed errors.
Tool use eliminates syntax errors; the semantic errors here come from the schema design, and dropping tool use would add syntax failures.

questoes.pergunta: In the automotive manufacturer's CI pipeline, the team converts legacy test descriptions to a new format with the Message Batches API. Last month it submitted all 8,000 at once: 31% failed validation, and two rounds of resubmission were needed. This month it first refined the prompt on 150 representative descriptions with synchronous calls, then submitted the full set, and 4% failed. Which statement about these results is correct?
opcoes: The gain came from the smaller resubmission volume, because the Batches API processes small batches faster and with fewer errors.
Refining the prompt on a sample before the full batch raised the first-pass success rate and avoided costly repeated resubmissions.
The sample run should also have used the Batches API, because running it synchronously cancels most of the savings the batch gives.
The 4% that failed show that batch processing is unreliable for this task, so each item should move to synchronous calls instead.
questoes.explicacao: Iterating on the prompt with a small representative sample is cheap and fast, and it fixes most failure causes before the large volume is submitted. That maximizes first-pass success and avoids paying for repeated resubmissions of thousands of items.
feedbacks: Batch size does not change output quality; the failure rate dropped because the prompt improved before submission.
Correct. Prompt refinement on a sample before batch processing raises first-pass success and cuts resubmission costs.
The sample is small, and fast synchronous feedback is what makes the refinement loop practical; batching it would add up to a day per iteration.
A 4% failure rate is normal residue that can be resubmitted by custom_id; switching everything to synchronous calls forfeits the savings for no gain.

questoes.pergunta: In the automotive manufacturer's CI pipeline, management asks for comprehensive tests for the legacy powertrain-control codebase: 400,000 lines, 6% coverage, and poorly documented dependencies between modules. An engineer proposes a nightly CI job that walks the source files in alphabetical order and generates tests for each one until coverage reaches 80%. How should you evaluate this proposal?
opcoes: Adopt it with parallel jobs per directory, so the whole codebase is covered in fewer nights while keeping the same file-by-file approach.
Adopt it, but order the files by size instead of alphabetically, so that the largest files, which hold the most logic, get tests first.
Reject it, and generate tests only for the files each pull request changes, so that coverage grows naturally as code is modified.
Reject it; first map the structure and find high-impact areas, then follow a prioritized plan that adapts as dependencies emerge.
questoes.explicacao: An open-ended task like adding comprehensive tests to a legacy codebase should be decomposed by first mapping the structure, identifying high-impact areas, and then building a prioritized plan that adapts as dependencies are discovered. An alphabetical walk spends effort without regard to risk or dependencies.
feedbacks: Parallelism speeds up the same unprioritized walk; it does not make the tests target the risky or central modules.
Size is a crude proxy for impact; large files can be generated tables while small modules sit on critical paths.
Testing changed files is a useful ongoing practice, but it leaves untouched legacy modules, often the riskiest, without tests indefinitely.
Correct. Map, prioritize by impact, and adapt the plan as dependencies surface.

questoes.pergunta: In the automotive manufacturer's CI pipeline, unit-test conventions apply to every *_test.cpp file, and these files sit next to the code in about 40 directories. Today the conventions are copied into a CLAUDE.md in each of those directories, the copies have drifted apart, and CI test reviews apply different rules in different directories. Which TWO changes best fix this? Choose TWO.
opcoes: Create a /test-conventions skill holding the conventions, and have engineers invoke it before writing or reviewing tests.
Remove the copied test conventions from the 40 directory CLAUDE.md files, keeping only conventions specific to each one.
Create .claude/rules/unit-tests.md with paths: ["**/*_test.cpp"] holding one copy of the conventions for all test files.
Move the conventions into the root CLAUDE.md, so that every CI job loads one shared copy at startup, whatever the file.
Add a CI step that copies the conventions into each directory's CLAUDE.md before each run, so that the copies never drift.
questoes.explicacao: Conventions for files spread across many directories fit a path-specific rule with a glob such as **/*_test.cpp, which applies by file type regardless of location. Once that single source exists, the duplicated copies in directory-level CLAUDE.md files should be removed so they cannot conflict with it.
feedbacks: A skill requires someone to invoke it, so CI reviews and engineers who forget would not get the conventions automatically.
Correct. Removing the drifting copies leaves the path-specific rule as the single source for test conventions.
Correct. One glob-scoped rule applies to every test file wherever it lives.
One copy stops the drift, but it loads the test conventions for every job and file, including non-test work, wasting context.
Syncing copies automates the wrong structure; directory files remain the mechanism even though the convention is not directory-bound.

questoes.pergunta: In the automotive manufacturer's CI pipeline, one Claude Code session generates unit tests for a changed module and then, in the same session, is asked to review whether those tests are meaningful. The review approves almost every test, yet mutation testing shows that 40% of the generated tests still pass when the code under test is deliberately broken. What is the most effective first step?
opcoes: Review the tests in a separate Claude Code invocation that sees the code and the tests but not the generation session's reasoning.
Enable extended thinking for the review step in the same session, so the model reasons longer before it approves each test.
Add an explicit instruction to the review prompt telling the model to be critical of its own tests and to assume some are weak.
Repeat the same-session review three times and reject any test that at least one of the three reviews marks as weak.
questoes.explicacao: A session that generated the tests keeps its own reasoning about why they are adequate, so it rarely questions them. An independent instance without that context reviews the tests on their merits and is more effective than self-review instructions or extended thinking in the same session.
feedbacks: Correct. An independent review instance does not share the generator's reasoning context.
Extended thinking still reasons from the same context that produced the tests, so it tends to reconfirm the original decisions.
Telling a model to doubt itself does not remove the generation reasoning it is anchored to; self-review stays weak.
Repeating a biased review multiplies cost while keeping the same bias; the three runs share the same context.

questoes.pergunta: In the automotive manufacturer's CI pipeline, every pull request to the brake-controller firmware gets the same review: check each changed file against the coding rules, check that the signal interfaces between changed modules still match, and write a summary for the safety engineer. The team is choosing how to structure this review. Which design fits best?
opcoes: A single prompt that receives each changed file and asks for the rule checks, interface checks, and summary together in one response.
An autonomous agent that decides at run time which checks to perform on each pull request, based on what it finds in the diff.
Per-file rule checks run in parallel, with the safety summary written directly from their results and no further step between them.
A fixed chain: a rule-check pass for each file, then a cross-file interface pass, then a summary step that draws on both results.
questoes.explicacao: The review steps are known in advance and the same for every pull request, so prompt chaining fits: a fixed sequence of focused steps, starting with per-file analysis, then a cross-file integration pass for the interfaces, then the summary. Dynamic decomposition is for open-ended investigations whose steps depend on findings.
feedbacks: One prompt doing all three tasks over every file dilutes attention and mixes local and cross-file concerns in a single pass.
Dynamic decomposition suits open-ended investigation; for a predictable review it adds variability and may skip required checks.
This drops the cross-file step, so interface mismatches between modules are never examined before the summary is written.
Correct. Prompt chaining with per-file and integration passes fits a predictable multi-aspect review.
